newsitem.title: CROATIA: Serbs seeking Croatian papers pelted with eggs.
newsitem.headline: Serbs seeking Croatian papers pelted with eggs.

text.p: Serb protesters in the enclave of Eastern Slavonia surrounded a U.N.-run office issuing Croatian government documents and threw eggs at compatriots applying for papers, U.N. officials said on Friday.
A group of local residents blocked the entrance to the office in Beli Manastir on Thursday, demanding its closure, said Yuri Chizhik of the U.N. Transitional Authority in Eastern Slavonia (UNTAES).
"They threw eggs and shouted abuse at Belgian soldiers safeguarding the building and at (Serb) visitors to the office," Chizhik told Reuters by telephone from Vukovar, main town in the enclave.
"The crowd grew hour by hour, and in the end there were some 500 people surrounding the building. A few applicants were also stranded inside," he said.
The crowd dispersed after UNTAES summoned local officials to resolve the stand-off.

Since August, Croatian officials have been regularly coming to the U.N. office in Beli Manastir to issue Croatian identity documents to local Serbs in preparation for Eastern Slavonia's transfer back to government rule in spring 1997.

Some of the roughly 130,000 Serbs in the region remain vehemently opposed to the restoration of Croatian authority, but no longer have the military means to prevent it following a U.N.-enforced dissolution of Serb militia.
Eastern Slavonia was one of three regions in Croatia seized by minority Serbs in a 1991 war against the country's move to independence from federal Yugoslavia.
Croatia recaptured two other Serb enclaves in a series of blitz offensives in 1995, leading to a mass exodus of Serb residents, thousands of whom ended up in Eastern Slavonia.
UNTAES, with 5,000 troops aty its disposal, took control of Eastern Slavonia in January with a mandate to prepare it for reintegration with Croatia.
It was originally given a one-year mandate, with possible extensions if difficulties arise. Local Serbs want to see the mission extended for another year to January 1998.
